content:
On September 21, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt “all permits sought by data centers” until state agencies finish auditing what those projects intend to draw from the power grid and the water supply. “Simply put, Texans must come first,” Abbott said in the directive. “Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects.”

But according to two watchdog groups that reviewed the agency’s own public records, the paperwork kept moving. Public Citizen and the FracTracker Alliance found 35 permitting actions for data center projects in the weeks after Abbott’s order, as reported by Inside Climate News: 14 applications fast-tracked or handed to engineers for review, 11 stormwater approvals, seven certified pollution estimates, and three public notices. The first actions came on September 22 — the day after Abbott’s order — when the agency mailed notices of preliminary approval to three major projects: NRG’s Prairie Energy Center, VoltaGrid’s ABI-1 power plant, and the Nexus self-powered data center in Hubbard, in Hill County. Stormwater approvals went to projects including Crusoe’s data center campus in Abilene, the Caldwell Valley Technology Park, and EdgeConneX’s Cedar Creek campus.

“Business as usual,” or business as ordered?

“The TCEQ’s own data indicates that it’s business as usual for data centers,” Kathryn Guerra of Public Citizen told the Texas Tribune. “Affected communities were promised a freeze, and instead what they’re getting is another reason to distrust the TCEQ.” The groups wrote: “These actions do not signal an agency trying to pause.”

Abbott’s office had an answer ready. Press secretary Andrew Mahaleris said the pause covered approving permits, not processing them. “No permits have been approved,” he said. Public Citizen counters that it identified at least six new stormwater construction permits tied to data centers that were approved after Abbott’s directive — and that the day after the watchdogs went public, the agency said those stormwater permits had been suspended. Critics note there is an obvious contradiction: you cannot suspend a permit that was never issued.

What this means for Webb County

This fight matters here. Data center developers have been circling South Texas, where land is cheap and the border economy keeps growing — and every one of those projects means enormous water and electricity demand on systems Webb County families already depend on. The Texas Tribune also reports that TCEQ has shut down its online permit-filing system in the wake of the controversy, and that Abbott has received $9 million in donations from data center developers and owners, according to 404 Media’s reporting of Tribune findings.

Only 28 percent of data centers responded to the state’s mandatory water-use survey, and Abbott has since directed the Texas Water Development Board to penalize projects that refuse to report. Meanwhile the ERCOT and Public Utility Commission audits of what data centers will draw from the grid are still unfinished — the very audits Abbott said must come before any permit moves forward. The question now is whether the “pause” was a policy or a headline.

Sources:

  • The Texas Tribune, republished: “Abbott Halts Data Center Permits Until Texas Knows What They Will Draw”
  • San Antonio Current: “Investigation finds Gov. Greg Abbott’s ‘pause’ on data centers isn’t a pause at all”
  • 404 Media: “‘It Ain’t Right:’ Texas Said It Would Halt Data Center Permits. The State is Pushing Ahead Anyway”
  • Inside Climate News reporting summarized: watchdogs find 35 permitting actions after the order
  • Particle: “Watchdogs Say Texas Continued Data-Center Permits After Abbott’s Pause”

Webb Watch 956
excerpt: Gov. Greg Abbott ordered Texas environmental regulators to halt all data-center permits on Sept. 21. Two watchdog groups reviewed the agency's own records and found 35 permitting actions moved forward afterward.
title: Abbott Ordered a Halt to 'All Permits' for Data Centers. Watchdogs Say the State Kept Issuing Them Anyway.
